growth_story.headline: St. Lucia's income per person rides tourism's swings: a collapse in 2020, a fast rebound, a new peak in 2024, then a slip as hotels closed.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 St. Lucia's growth shows no lasting shift: income per person grew 1.4 percent a year on average over 1990–2025, one long era rather than several. Inside that era the year-to-year swings are large: their standard deviation over the last 20 years, 7.7, sits at the 91st percentile of all economies. As bananas lost the value of their protected access to Europe from the early 1990s, tourism became the main growth sector, but a hurricane in 2007 and slumps in arrivals kept growth uneven, and income per person grew only 0.9 percent a year over 2006–2015. The pandemic cut income per person by 23.2 percent in 2020, in one of the largest falls in the region, before a tourism rebound lifted it 11.0 percent in 2021 and 19.2 percent in 2022. It reached a new peak of about 12,191 constant US dollars in 2024, up from 8,418 in 1990, and growth over 2016–2025 averaged 2.1 percent a year, close to the structural-peer median of 2.2. In 2025 hotel closures and fewer flights cut tourist arrivals, leaving income per person 0.8 percent below that peak.

threads.title: Bananas give way to tourism
threads.text: For about three decades, bananas sold to Europe under trade preferences gave the eastern Caribbean islands, St. Lucia among them, valuable support. The value of those preferences fell sharply from the early 1990s, banana exports declined, and tourism, backed by rising foreign investment, became the main source of growth.

threads.title: Storms in the hurricane belt
threads.text: The island sits in the hurricane belt, and storms have knocked back output. In 2007 a hurricane hit banana exports and activity stalled; the World Bank still names recurrent climate shocks as a source of volatile growth.

threads.title: Pandemic collapse, tourism rebound
threads.text: When travel stopped in 2020, income per person fell 23.2 percent. The return of visitors drove a sharp recovery, and by 2022 income per person was back above its 2019 level of about 11,078 constant US dollars.

citations.title: St. Lucia: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/3)
citations.quote: After one of the largest declines in the region in 2020, economic growth rebounded sharply, buoyed by increased tourism services.

threads.title: Slow catch-up, heavy debt
threads.text: Behind the swings, the IMF describes income per person drifting further behind the United States over past decades, with weak productivity and high public debt. The World Bank adds weak infrastructure and limited access to credit, and says exposure to shocks has compounded these problems.

citations.quote: Exposure to shocks has weighed on growth and job creation, compounding structural challenges, including high public debt, infrastructure weaknesses, and limited access to credit.

since_last_year.text: The closure of two large hotels and fewer flights cut tourist arrivals in 2025, and the World Bank now estimates the economy shrank that year. Construction, farming and manufacturing softened the fall, and arrivals picked up again in the first half of 2026.

citations.quote: Real GDP contracted by 0.6 percent in 2025, largely reflecting a 2.1 percent fall in stay-over arrivals due to the closure of two major hotels

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Saint Lucia (October 2026)
citations.quote: Tourism flows recovered in the first half of 2026, as stay-over arrivals rose by 2.5 percent compared with the same period in 2025.

growth_story.tension: The IMF, writing in late 2025, called recent performance robust and expected the economy to keep growing that year on the back of construction. The World Bank's later estimate shows a contraction, and the data show income per person slipping to 0.8 percent below its 2024 peak. The strong rebound since 2020 also sits inside a long record of just 1.4 percent a year since 1990, the slow catch-up the IMF itself describes.
